content:
Hand osteoarthritis can make buttons, zips, jars, taps and kettles hard work, but small changes usually help a lot. Warm your hands before you start, sit down to dress, choose looser clothes with front fastenings or elastic, and use simple aids such as a button hook, zip pull, jar opener, lever taps and thick-handled cutlery. Daily hand exercises and pacing keep your hands working, and a splint, a pharmacist's advice on pain relief or an occupational therapist can help when grip is getting harder. See your GP for a hot, swollen joint, numbness or tingling, or if your hands are getting worse quickly. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

This guide is about getting dressed, washed and fed when hand osteoarthritis makes grip hard. For cooking in more depth, see cooking with arthritis. For pain at the base of the thumb, see thumb base pain. If tablets and blister packs are the problem, see dosette boxes and pill packs with sore hands.

What hand osteoarthritis does to grip

Osteoarthritis in the hands most often affects the joints nearest the fingertips, the middle finger joints and the base of the thumb. The NHS describes pain, stiffness, knobbly swellings and difficulty with fine tasks. Pinching (turning a key, doing up a button) and twisting (jars, taps, bottle tops) tend to hurt most, and grip strength can drop when you use your hands less. Many people find the stiffness is worst first thing and after a lot of use.

Start the day gently

  • Warm your hands in a bowl of warm water, or run them under the warm tap, before you dress.
  • Do a few gentle hand movements: make a loose fist, open the hand wide, touch each fingertip to the thumb.
  • Leave fiddly tasks until later in the morning when your hands have loosened up.

Easier dressing

  • Sit down to dress on a firm chair or the edge of the bed, with clothes laid out in order.
  • Choose easier clothes: looser tops that go over the head, elasticated waists, front-fastening or soft stretch bras, wrap skirts, and cardigans with larger buttons.
  • Buttons: a button hook pulls buttons through for you. You can also have buttons sewn on with elastic thread, or swap them for magnetic fastenings or hook-and-loop tape.
  • Zips: add a ring or loop to the zip pull so you can hook a finger through it.
  • Shoes and socks: slip-on shoes with a firm back, elastic laces or hook-and-loop straps, a long-handled shoehorn, and a sock aid if bending is also hard.
  • Jewellery and watches: magnetic clasps and stretch straps save a lot of fiddling.

Washing and grooming

  • Use pump bottles for soap, shampoo and toothpaste rather than squeezing tubes or twisting caps.
  • An electric toothbrush or a toothbrush with a thicker handle is easier to hold. You can build up handles yourself with foam tubing from a mobility shop or online.
  • Lever taps are much easier than twist taps. A tap turner can help with the taps you have.
  • A long-handled sponge or a towelling robe saves reaching and wringing.

In the kitchen

  • Opening: a jar opener or a rubber jar grip, ring-pull tins or an electric tin opener, and scissors with spring-open handles for packets.
  • Lifting: a lighter kettle, or a kettle tipper so you tilt rather than lift, or a hot water dispenser. Lightweight pans with two handles let you use both hands.
  • Chopping: buy food ready-chopped or frozen, or use a knife with an angled or thick handle and a spiked board to hold food still.
  • Carrying: slide things along the worktop or use a trolley rather than carrying them.
  • Sitting: a perching stool lets you prepare food sitting down.

Our guide to cooking with arthritis has more ideas, including easy meals.

Protect your hands as you go

Joint protection is about doing the same tasks with less strain on painful joints:

  • Use bigger joints where you can, for example carrying a bag over your forearm or shoulder rather than in your fingers.
  • Use two hands to lift, and keep heavy things close to your body.
  • Avoid gripping tightly for long spells. Take short breaks and switch tasks.
  • Spread jobs across the day and the week, rather than doing everything at once.

See joint protection for everyday tasks for the full approach.

Keep your hands working

NICE NG226 says exercise is a core treatment for osteoarthritis, including in the hands, alongside information and support to manage it. Gentle daily hand exercises help keep the joints moving and your grip stronger. Start with hand exercises for arthritis and, when you are ready, grip strength exercises. A little discomfort during exercise is normal; ease off if pain is much worse the next day.

Pain relief, splints and warmth

  • Warmth often eases stiff hands: warm water, a wheat bag (follow the heating instructions) or gloves in cold weather.
  • Ask a pharmacist whether an anti-inflammatory gel is suitable for you. Our guide to anti-inflammatory gels in later life explains who they suit.
  • A splint for the base of the thumb can ease pain during tasks. Ask your GP about a referral to a hand therapist, occupational therapist or physiotherapist, who can fit one and show you how to use it.

Where to get help

  • Your GP can confirm what is going on, discuss pain relief and refer you to physiotherapy, occupational therapy or hand therapy.
  • An occupational therapist looks at the tasks you find hard and suggests equipment and different ways of doing them. See occupational therapy for arthritis.
  • Your council can do a free care needs assessment. The NHS says equipment and small adaptations will be provided for free if you are assessed as needing them.
  • Many aids are also sold cheaply in pharmacies and mobility shops. See gadgets and aids for arthritis.

When to see a GP

  • A finger or wrist joint becomes hot, red and very swollen, especially if you feel unwell or have a temperature: get a same-day appointment or contact NHS 111.
  • Numbness, tingling or pins and needles in the fingers, especially at night, which can be carpal tunnel syndrome.
  • Swelling of the knuckles or wrists with long-lasting morning stiffness, which can be a sign of inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis rather than osteoarthritis.
  • Your hands are getting worse quickly, or you can no longer manage everyday tasks.
  • Call 999 for sudden weakness or numbness down one side of the body, a drooping face or slurred speech.

For family and carers

Offer to set things up rather than take tasks over: swap caps for easy-open tops, loosen jars before you leave, and put everyday items where they are easy to reach. Doing things with less effort keeps independence for longer.

Common questions

Will using my hands make osteoarthritis worse?

No. Using your hands and exercising them helps. What helps most is avoiding long spells of tight gripping and spreading heavy tasks out.

Are the knobbly lumps on my fingers dangerous?

Bony swellings near the finger joints are common in hand osteoarthritis. They can be sore while they form and usually settle. See your GP if a joint is hot, red and very swollen.

Do compression gloves help?

Some people find them comfortable, especially in cold weather. There is not strong evidence that they change osteoarthritis, so try them only if they help you.
